question: What does the petroleum and oil & gas sector in Uganda consist of across its value chain?
answer: Uganda's petroleum and oil & gas sector value chain is structured into three distinct operational segments: 1) Upstream — covers the acquisition of exploration rights, geological exploration, well appraisal, oilfield development (e.g. Tilenga and Kingfisher projects), commercial crude production, and environmental decommissioning; 2) Midstream — encompasses the transportation of crude oil via the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP), petroleum refining, natural gas processing, and liquefaction/conversion; 3) Downstream — involves the importation, distribution, marketing, and retail sale of refined white and black petroleum products (petrol, diesel, kerosene, aviation fuel, lubricants, and LPG) through licensed oil marketing companies and fuel service stations equipped with Electronic Dispenser Controllers (EDCs).

question: How do petroleum, oil, and gas businesses register with government agencies and URA in Uganda?
answer: All petroleum sector entities operating in Uganda must undergo mandatory multi-agency registration: 1) Business Registration: Uganda Registration Services Bureau (URSB) for company incorporation, Memorandum and Articles of Association, and Form 20; 2) Sector Licensing & Regulation: Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development (MEMD) for exploration/production licenses, and the Petroleum Authority of Uganda (PAU) for regulatory oversight and National Supplier Database (NSD) accreditation; 3) Tax Registration: Uganda Revenue Authority (URA) via portal.ura.go.ug to acquire a 10-digit TIN with obligations for Corporation Tax (CIT), PAYE, VAT, Withholding Tax, and Excise Duty; 4) Downstream Retail: Municipal trading licenses and fuel dispensing permits.

question: What taxes apply to oil and gas miners, contractors, and downstream fuel dealers in Uganda?
answer: The applicable statutory taxes in the petroleum sector include: 1) Corporation Income Tax (CIT): 30% of chargeable income (gross income less allowable deductions); 2) Withholding Tax (WHT): 10% on service payments made by licensees to non-resident contractors for upstream field services, 6% standard WHT on local suppliers (unless exempt under Section 119(5)(f) ITA), and 15% on interest/dividends; 3) Branch Profit Tax (BPT): 15% on repatriated profits of foreign corporate branches under Section 82 ITA; 4) Value Added Tax (VAT): 18% standard rate with mandatory EFRIS fiscalization; fuel dealers are statutorily required to integrate Electronic Dispenser Controllers (EDCs) at pump nozzles to automatically transmit real-time fiscal receipts; 5) Excise Duty on Fuel: Levied as a specific tax per liter of petrol, diesel, and kerosene, withheld and remitted monthly by oil marketing companies; 6) PAYE: Deducted from employee compensation above the monthly threshold.

question: What statutory tax incentives and deemed VAT provisions apply to oil and gas contractors and licensees in Uganda?
answer: Uganda provides extensive tax incentives to the petroleum sector under the Income Tax Act, VAT Act, and EACCMA: 1) Customs Exemption: EACCMA Fifth Schedule Part B Item 30(a) exempts import duty, VAT, and levies on equipment, inputs, and machinery for direct and exclusive use in oil, gas, or geothermal exploration upon MEMD/PAU recommendation (excluding non-specialized passenger vehicles); 2) Deemed VAT Provisions: Under Section 24(5) VAT Act (effective July 2015), VAT charged by a contractor to a licensed oil operator is deemed paid, meaning the contractor does not remit this VAT to URA; 3) Full Input VAT Credit on Imported Services: Under Section 28(1)(b) VAT Act, oil licensees and contractors receive 100% input credit on imported services, resulting in net zero VAT; 4) VAT Cash Refunds: Under Section 42(1) VAT Act, contractors receive prompt cash refunds for local input VAT; 5) Uncapped Loss Carry-Forward: Sections 89GA(2) and (3) ITA permit indefinite loss carry-forward without expiration; 6) Accelerated Capital Allowances: Immediate accelerated depreciation under Sections 89GB, 89GC, and 89GD ITA.

question: What specific tax incentives and exemptions are granted to the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) project?
answer: Under the EACOP (Special Provisions) Act, Host Government Agreement (HGA), and Intergovernmental Agreement (IGA), the EACOP project benefits from a dedicated fiscal regime: 1) Income Tax: 10-year Corporate Income Tax holiday for the EACOP Project Company; WHT on interest to related lenders reduced to 10% (0% for independent lenders); 5% WHT on non-resident technical service fees; 0% WHT on EACOP dividends and equipment imports; 2) Value Added Tax: Statutory right to VAT registration; 0% VAT on pipeline transportation and incidental transit services; 0% VAT on EACOP goods/service imports and crude export sales; Deemed VAT applies on supplies between Level 2 contractors, Level 1 contractors, and the Project Company, with cash refunds for Level 2 local VAT; 3) Customs & Excise: Total exemption from customs duties, AU levy, and EAC infrastructure levy on capital goods; no security bonds for temporary imports or crude transit; zero excise duty on project supplies; 4) Stamp Duty: 100% exemption on Project Company share transfers; land acquisition and financing transfer instruments capped at a nominal UGX 10,000 flat stamp duty; 5) Municipal/Regulatory Levies: Zero transit fees and an aggregate USD 100,000 annual cap on all local council, trade license, and regulatory fees.

question: How does URA administer taxes and VAT refunds for petroleum licensees, contractors, and EACOP transactions?
answer: URA administers the petroleum industry through a dedicated Petroleum Division within the Domestic Taxes Department at URA Headquarters (Nakawa). The division features specialized tax audit, policy, and revenue accounting teams focused on upstream oil licensees (TotalEnergies EP Uganda, CNOOC Uganda, UNOC) and Tier-1/Tier-2 contractors. Additionally, URA operates a dedicated fast-track EACOP Help Desk to expedite pipeline documentation, fast-track custom clearances at border stations, verify deemed VAT schedules, and ensure accelerated turnaround of statutory VAT cash refunds.
